questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A criterion and the observable behind it
questions.learningObjective: identify what a rubric criterion needs before it can be applied consistently
questions.stem: A rubric's criterion for one section of an essay reads: shows independent judgement. What has to sit beside it before a marker can apply it consistently?

options.text: An observable indication of that judgement in the submitted text, since what cannot be pointed to is applied differently each time
A statement of how many marks the section carries, since a weighting is what a criterion is chiefly for
options.misconception: confuses how much a criterion counts for with what it would count, and the two can come apart entirely

options.text: A list of the readings the judgement is drawn from, since no criterion can call itself independent of them
options.misconception: supplies the source list a criterion does not need in order to be applied to a text

options.text: A model answer, since a criterion is only reliable when the exemplary work is on the desk beside it
options.misconception: believes consistency requires an exemplar, when markers apply the same judgement without one and still agree

questions.explanation: A criterion is a rule for reading a text, and a rule that names an impression rather than an indication in the text will be applied according to the marker's mood on the day, which is the problem a rubric exists to solve. The first option names the observable. The second supplies a weighting, which is a separate decision about how much a section counts and does not tell a marker what to look for. The third attaches a reading list, which the assignment may well set and the criterion does not need. The fourth makes an exemplar the condition of consistency, and a criterion strong enough to need one has not been written as a criterion.
questions.hint: Ask what a marker would point at in the text to show the judgement is there.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a rubric level describes
questions.learningObjective: state what distinguishes one level of a rubric from the level below it
questions.stem: A rubric has four levels for one criterion, named developing, competent, secure, and outstanding. What is each level's description for?

options.text: The observable difference in the work between that level and the one below, since a level is defined by what changes when the work reaches it
The number of marks attached to it, since a level and a mark band are two names for the same thing
options.misconception: equates a description of work with a number, which is what a level can be converted into rather than what it is

options.text: The length of the work that falls in it, since a fuller treatment of the same question is what a higher level amounts to
options.misconception: uses length as the difference, and a longer treatment can add nothing that a shorter one lacked

options.text: The number of sources cited, since a wider reading is what separates the higher levels from the lower ones
options.misconception: makes a count of sources the difference, which measures reading done rather than judgement shown

questions.explanation: A level is a step, and a step is defined by the difference it makes, so the description of a level says what a reader can see in the work that was not there at the level below. The first option says that. The second makes a level a number, which is a conversion a marking scheme may perform afterwards and not the description a marker uses. The third and fourth offer measurable substitutes, and both measure the size of an input rather than the quality of a performance. Length and source count do move with level on average, which is why they are tempting, and a well-written essay with three sources and a thin one with thirty are the two texts that break the pattern.
questions.hint: Ask what a marker would see in the work at one level and not at the one below.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Improvement as the thing being marked
questions.learningObjective: identify what a criterion comparing a student with their own earlier work makes depend on that earlier work
questions.stem: A course rubric awards credit for a term essay only where it improves on the student's own previous one, and reports that most of the class submitted something weaker than their first attempt. What does that criterion make depend on?

options.text: The student's earlier work, so a strong first attempt counts against a strong second one and a weak first one flatters a weak second one
The standard of judgement, which the course has effectively lowered for everyone who wrote well the first time
options.misconception: frames the design as a change in the standard rather than as a change in what the work is compared with

options.text: The number of drafts a student has kept, so the class result records how much material a student had to hand rather than how well they wrote
options.misconception: makes the criterion a measure of retained drafts, which it never mentions

options.text: Nothing, since a criterion that compares a student with their own earlier work measures the two texts the same way
options.misconception: believes a comparison is neutral because both texts pass through the same comparison, which is what erases the difference between them

questions.explanation: Comparing a submission with a student's earlier one makes the earlier text part of what is being marked, and the two texts are judged by their relation rather than each on its own, so a class of good first drafts will produce a class of unremarkable second ones. The first option names that. The second describes the design as a change in standards, which is a different complaint and would call for a different remedy. The third supplies a fact about drafts that the criterion never invokes. The fourth thinks a shared comparison is a neutral one, and the whole effect of the criterion comes from the comparison, not in spite of it.
questions.hint: Ask what the mark would be if the first attempt had been the weak one instead.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A criterion no submission can meet
questions.learningObjective: recognise a rubric criterion that the stated work cannot satisfy
questions.stem: A criterion asks that the essay engage every position in the field, including those the word limit leaves no room for. What follows from that pairing?

options.text: No submission at the stated length can meet it, so the criterion separates no one and carries no information about any of them
It is a demanding but fair standard, since a criterion only counts when it is beyond the reach of most work
options.misconception: mistakes an unmeetable criterion for a high one, and a high criterion is still met by the best work

options.text: It should be read as an ideal and marked leniently, so the criterion keeps its ambition while the marks stay fair
options.misconception: keeps a criterion the length of the work cannot satisfy and lets the marks quietly depart from it

options.text: It states the course's aims rather than a standard, so no mark should be made to depend on it at all
options.misconception: relabels the criterion as an aim and excuses the marking rather than fixing the criterion

questions.explanation: A criterion is a description of work, and it can only describe work that is possible at the length the assignment allows, so a criterion demanding engagement with more than can be fitted into the essay is not a high standard but an absent one: no submission can meet it and no submission fails it. The first option says that. The second confuses ambition with impossibility, and the difference is whether the best available work could satisfy the criterion. The third keeps a criterion and then marks against something else, which leaves two documents describing the same assignment. The fourth reclassifies the criterion as an aim, which is available whenever a marker wants to avoid the question of feasibility.
questions.hint: Ask whether the best submission anyone could write at that length would satisfy the criterion.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A criterion every submission meets
questions.learningObjective: recognise a rubric criterion that carries no information about the work
questions.stem: A rubric awards full marks for any section written in continuous prose. What is wrong with that criterion?

options.text: Nothing in it separates a strong submission from a weak one, so the marks it carries record a formatting choice rather than a quality
Prose form is a legitimate requirement, since how an essay is presented is part of its quality
options.misconception: defends the criterion without answering that the requirement is met by work of any quality whatever

options.text: It rewards conformity, since continuous prose is easier to mark consistently than a broken form
options.misconception: turns a criterion that carries no information into a merit of consistency, which is a property of the marking not of the work

options.text: It becomes acceptable if it carries few marks, since a small weighting limits how much a weak signal can do
options.misconception: believes a weighting repairs a criterion that has no signal in it at any weight

questions.explanation: A criterion is worth marks to the extent that meeting it tells you something about the work, and a requirement met by every submission, of any quality, tells you nothing about any of them, so its marks are a flat charge applied to the set. The first option says that. The second argues for the requirement on general grounds and never returns to what it distinguishes. The third recasts the problem as one of marking convenience, and easier marking is a real concern that is not the concern here. The fourth offers a weighting as a remedy, and a signal that is absent cannot be recovered by turning it down.
questions.hint: Ask whether any two submissions of very different quality would be treated differently by this criterion.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a set of weightings rewards
questions.learningObjective: predict the student behaviour a pair of weightings most rewards
questions.stem: A rubric carries seventy per cent of the marks for gathering sources and thirty per cent for the argument those sources support. Which response is the weighting most likely to produce?

options.text: Gathering more sources than the argument needs, since the return on one more source is far higher than the return on a sharper argument
Sharpening the argument, since thirty per cent of the marks fall on what a reader of the finished work will notice
options.misconception: reasons from the intrinsic worth of the two features rather than from what the weighting pays for them

options.text: Splitting the work evenly between the two, since a student who reads the rubric will aim to match the two weights
options.misconception: assumes students allocate effort to match weights, when effort follows what effort buys

options.text: Taking whichever of the two is less work, since thirty per cent is a smaller commitment than seventy per cent
options.misconception: reads a weighting as a measure of how much work a task involves

questions.explanation: A weighting is a price, and where one of two things is worth more than twice what the other is worth the cheaper route to marks is the one that pays, so a student reasoning from the rubric adds sources rather than revising the argument the sources are meant to support. The first option says that. The second compares the two features on their merits, which is a reasonable view of what the assignment is for and not a prediction of what the marks do. The third assumes effort is matched to weights, which would be a strange thing to do when one return is twice the other. The fourth treats the weighting as a workload measure, and the weights say what counts, not what takes longest.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two uses of an hour would earn more marks.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Self-assessment without a shared reference point
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a calibration problem in self-assessment
questions.stem: Two students mark the same draft as excellent and as competent, and the course marker later puts it at the level the rubric calls developing. What does the pair of self-marks show?

options.text: That each student rated the draft against an imagined standard rather than against the level descriptions, since the same text came out at opposite ends
That self-assessment does not belong in a course and should be replaced by a second marker
options.misconception: proposes removing the activity instead of calibrating it against a shared description

options.text: That the two drafts differed more than the two students realised, since one scale produced such different results
options.misconception: reads two ratings of one text as though two texts had been rated

options.text: That the students know their own work better than the marker can, since their judgements differ from the marker's
options.misconception: treats disagreement with the marker as a sign of self-knowledge rather than of a different reference point

questions.explanation: Self-assessment is a comparison against a description, and when the same text is called excellent by one reader and competent by another while a third calls it developing, the three are applying three different standards rather than three different amounts of care. The first option names the diagnosis, and the presence of a marker's level description in the case is what makes it visible. The second throws out the activity instead of supplying it with the reference point it lacks. The third supposes two texts where the case has one, so the divergence has nowhere to go. The fourth turns a disagreement with the marker into a virtue, and the two students disagree with each other as well as with the marker.
questions.hint: Ask what the three ratings were each measured against.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Scores that follow a relationship rather than a text
questions.learningObjective: interpret a marking pattern as evidence about relationships rather than about merit
questions.stem: In peer marking, the two friends in the set exchange the highest scores, and the pair who openly disliked each other exchange the lowest, while every essay was allocated to a marker at random. What is the best reading of the pattern?

options.text: That the scores follow the relationship rather than the text, since random allocation left the essay as the only thing constant across the pairs
That the friends wrote the stronger essays, since the top scores in a set are usually earned
options.misconception: credits merit that random allocation was in a position to have shown or hidden independently of the pairing

options.text: That the allocation was not random after all, since friendship is a good predictor of who is placed together
options.misconception: suggests a fault in the allocation, which the case has already excluded by design

options.text: That peer marking is unreliable as a method, since a relationship should never touch a score
options.misconception: dismisses the method from a pattern that random allocation has already made informative

questions.explanation: Random allocation is what makes this pattern legible: because the essays were not chosen to suit the pairs, the only thing the scores can be tracking is who was reading, and a ranking that follows the relationships is evidence about the marking rather than about the essays. The first option says that. The second reads the ranking as merit, and merit would have been distributed the same way whatever the pairing. The third proposes a fault in the allocation that the design rules out. The fourth dismisses the method, and a method that produces a relationship-shaped pattern has revealed something about how people mark, which is a use for it rather than an argument against it.
questions.hint: Ask what the allocation procedure held constant and what it left free to vary.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A grade and the reason attached to it
questions.learningObjective: state what makes a grade answerable rather than merely consistent
questions.stem: What makes a grade defensible in a way a mark total on its own is not?

options.text: A stated reason connecting the mark to something in the submitted work, so a reader can check the mark against what was read
The total, since a total is arithmetic and arithmetic is not open to argument
options.misconception: treats the sum as self-justifying and leaves the judgements that produced it unstated

options.text: The marker's consistency across submissions, so a mark that matches the marker's other work is defensible in itself
options.misconception: makes consistency the warrant, and a consistently applied reading can be consistently wrong

options.text: The agreement of a second marker, since two readers reaching one mark settles what the work supports
options.misconception: takes agreement as the warrant, when two markers can agree on a reading the text does not bear

questions.explanation: A defensible mark is one a student can be shown the reasoning behind, and the reasoning has to point at something in the work, since without that the mark is a verdict rather than a reading. The first option says that. The second makes arithmetic into a defence, and a total is a sum of judgements, not a substitute for them. The third and fourth both offer agreement rather than a reason, and consistency or second-marker agreement can certify that a reading was applied evenly without showing that the work supports it.
questions.hint: Ask what a student would need in order to disagree with the mark on grounds.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A comment that tells the student what to do next
questions.learningObjective: recognise a comment that carries an operation rather than only a fault
questions.stem: A comment reads: the second paragraph moves from the survey result to the claim without showing the step, so rewrite that paragraph to state the rule that would take you from the number to the claim. What does this comment do that a fault report does not?

options.text: It names the place, the fault, and the operation that would repair it, so the student knows what to carry out rather than what went wrong
It identifies the fault precisely, so the student can be left to work out the repair
options.misconception: treats naming a fault as the whole of feedback and leaves the operation out

options.text: It attends to one paragraph closely, so the rest of the essay needs no further comment
options.misconception: turns attention to one place into permission to leave the rest unexamined

options.text: It calls for a rewrite, so the text as it stands does not need reading again
options.misconception: treats a suggested operation as a judgement that the existing writing is finished with

questions.explanation: A comment is useful to the extent that a student can act on it, and a comment becomes actionable when it names where the problem is, what the problem is, and what operation would address it, which is what the third clause does by asking for a rule rather than for more words. The first option says that. The second stops one clause short and hands the hardest part back to the student, which is the part they are least equipped to do. The third draws a conclusion about the rest of the essay that the comment says nothing about. The fourth reads a request for a change as a verdict on the current text, and the request is the opposite: it says the current text is not yet finished.
questions.hint: Ask what the student would have to work out for themselves after reading the comment.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A comment that names a fault and stops
questions.learningObjective: identify what is missing from a comment that reports a deficiency without an operation
questions.stem: A comment says the second paragraph lacks a link between the evidence and the claim. What has that comment left out?

options.text: An operation the student could carry out, so the comment reports what is missing without telling the student how to supply it
A quotation from the paragraph, since a criticism should be anchored in the words it applies to
options.misconception: asks for the anchoring the comment largely supplies already by naming the paragraph

options.text: A comparison with other submissions, since a fault has meaning only relative to the standard of the set
options.misconception: supposes a fault is defined by the set, when a fault is defined by the claim the work was meant to support

options.text: The number of marks lost, so the reader can see the cost of the deficiency
options.misconception: asks for a figure to be repeated where the missing element is a way of working

questions.explanation: Reporting a deficiency tells the student where the work stops being adequate and leaves them to invent the remedy, and inventing the remedy is the part of revision that a student least able to revise needs help with, so a comment that names a fault without an operation transfers the difficult step back to the person who submitted it. The first option says that. The second asks for a quotation, and the comment has already located itself in a paragraph. The third makes a fault relative to the set, which would leave the criterion doing nothing except ranking. The fourth asks for a mark to be restated, which is a matter of the mark scheme rather than of the comment's usefulness.
questions.hint: Ask whether the student could carry out something specific after reading it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Feedback that arrives after the assessed work is closed
questions.learningObjective: state what late feedback can and cannot do for the work it comments on
questions.stem: A student submits a draft three days after the date set for feedback, and the feedback returns after the final submission deadline. What follows for that feedback?

options.text: It can no longer change the assessed work, so it functions as advice about the next piece rather than as input to this one
The work should not be marked, since it arrived after the date the course set for it
options.misconception: moves the question to the marking of late work and leaves the feedback's own timing untouched

options.text: It should be supplied in full regardless of date, since the student's need for feedback does not change with the calendar
options.misconception: answers a question about entitlement as though the question were one of need

options.text: The three days should be added to the student's later deadlines, since the delay is why the feedback arrived late
options.misconception: treats a missed feedback window as though it created time in the assessment schedule

questions.explanation: Feedback functions by being acted on, and once the assessed work is closed no comment on it can be acted on within that work, which is a fact about the sequence rather than about the quality of the comment. The first option says that, and it also implies the only use left, which is to inform the next piece. The second relocates the problem to late work, a real question with its own rules. The third answers a question about entitlement and treats the schedule as though it did not exist. The fourth tries to buy back the missing time, and a delay in the feedback window has not created any time in the assessment itself.
questions.hint: Ask which submission the comment could still change.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A comment read as the opposite of what it says
questions.learningObjective: identify the misreading a student's revision makes of a specific comment
questions.stem: A comment reads: the opening is clear, but the claim it sets up is one the evidence in the second half cannot support, so the paragraph stating the claim will need to change. The student keeps the opening and adds three sources to the second half. What has the student done?

options.text: Treated the comment as a request for more evidence behind the claim, when it identified the claim as the thing to be changed
Treated the comment as a criticism of the opening, when it praised the opening and questioned the claim instead
options.misconception: invents a reading of the praise as criticism, which the comment's wording does not support

options.text: Carried out what the comment asked, since supporting a claim is what a comment about support requires
options.misconception: calls the misreading compliance and so removes the need to explain the divergence

options.text: Found the comment unclear, since a comment that praises one paragraph and questions another cannot be acted on
options.misconception: attributes the divergence to the comment's wording, which names both operations distinctly

questions.explanation: The comment names two things and asks for a change to the second: the claim is the problem and the evidence is what stands behind it, so the operations available were to narrow the claim or to find evidence that would carry it. The student heard only a demand for support and acted on that, which is a common reading and not an unreasonable one to reach from a vague comment. The first option identifies it. The second supplies a reading of the praise that the wording does not invite. The third calls the divergence compliance, and compliance would have produced a different edit. The fourth puts the fault in the comment, and the comment does say which paragraph will need to change.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two things the comment names was treated as the problem.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a revision memo has to carry
questions.learningObjective: choose the combination of contents that makes a revision memo useful to a reader
questions.stem: A revision memo accompanies a resubmitted essay. Which combination of contents serves the memo's purpose?

options.text: What the earlier draft claimed, what the feedback questioned, what was changed in response, and what was left unchanged with a reason
A list of the changes made and the number of words added, since a memo is primarily a record of activity
options.misconception: records how much writing happened rather than what the feedback changed about the argument

options.text: A short defence of the earlier draft and a summary of the new one, since the memo presents the author's work
options.misconception: makes the memo a second submission rather than a record of what the feedback did

options.text: The feedback quoted in full and the resubmitted text attached, since the memo's job is to carry both documents
options.misconception: reproduces the two documents whose comparison the memo is supposed to make possible

questions.explanation: A memo exists so that a reader can see what the feedback did to the work, which needs four things: the earlier claim, the objection, the response, and an account of what was left alone, since a memo that lists only changes conceals the feedback the student decided to ignore. The first option contains all four. The second makes it an activity log, and word counts say nothing about whether the objection was met. The third turns it into a second piece of writing to be assessed, and a defence of the earlier draft is the opposite of what the assignment asked for. The fourth attaches the documents and leaves the comparison to the reader, which is the work the memo was asked to do.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader could not work out from the two drafts alone.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a piece of a portfolio actually evidences
questions.learningObjective: match a portfolio piece to the criterion it can evidence
questions.stem: A portfolio includes a two-page summary of a project the student did not design. What does that piece evidence?

options.text: The student's account of the project, which is evidence of how well the student can describe work rather than of how the student works
The student's judgement, since deciding how to present someone else's project is itself a design decision
options.misconception: credits the piece with evidencing design where the piece is a description of another's design

options.text: Nothing, since a piece the student did not produce cannot be assessed at all
options.misconception: dismisses a piece that can be assessed for a narrower criterion than the one it was offered for

options.text: The student's part in the project, since a summary shows what the student was able to take from it
options.misconception: infers a contribution to a project the case states the student had none in

questions.explanation: A portfolio criterion says what a piece is being offered as evidence of, and a summary of someone else's project is evidence of description: it can show whether the student can represent a project accurately and in a form a reader can follow, and it cannot show whether the student could run one. The first option names the criterion this piece fits. The second makes presentation a design decision in itself, and choosing an account is not the same as making the thing. The third rules the piece out entirely, and it can be assessed for what it does show. The fourth invents a contribution the case has already excluded.
questions.hint: Ask what the student did that the piece would reveal if it were absent.

questions.topic: What an oral presentation puts in front of a marker
questions.learningObjective: identify the capacity an oral presentation tests that written work does not
questions.stem: A student presents a design for eight minutes, is asked how it would fail, and replies that the question was not in the brief. The marker notes that the student had not considered failure at any point in the design. What has the presentation brought out?

options.text: That the student cannot bring the design's own weaknesses into view when nobody has set them out in front of them
That the student can meet an eight-minute limit, since the presentation was delivered within the time given
options.misconception: answers with something the case establishes and that says nothing about the design

options.text: That the student is prepared to challenge the marker's premise, since refusing an unbriefed question is defensible
options.misconception: recasts a gap in the design as a position, which the marker's note contradicts

options.text: That the marking scheme fails to anticipate questions outside the brief, so the situation itself is at fault
options.misconception: raises a scheme problem where the case records a gap in the student's account of the design

questions.explanation: An oral presentation tests something a paper does not, because the marker can ask the one question the prepared script has no answer to, and here the answer showed that the design had been built without a thought about failure at all. The first option names that. The second reports a fact the case supplies and that bears on nothing. The third offers a sympathetic reading of an answer the marker's note explains, and a refusal to answer is not the same as a challenge to the premise. The fourth makes the scheme the problem, when what was missing was a consideration in the design.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What an examination under time pressure requires
questions.learningObjective: state what a timed written examination chiefly demands, then what follows for course practice
questions.stem: A written examination gives two hours for six questions on material read three months earlier. First say what such an examination chiefly demands, then say what follows for how the course prepares students.

options.text: That the material can be recalled and used under time pressure, and that practice at recall under time pressure has to take place during the course
That the material has been understood in depth, and that early feedback on written work is what builds that understanding
options.misconception: confuses what an examination measures with what the course should develop, and the two are separable

options.text: That the six questions can be divided fairly among the two hours, and that the scheme should publish how it divides them
options.misconception: makes the division the difficulty, which students do not control and markers do resolve in the scheme

options.text: That the student can read quickly, and that the course should set more reading for the same period
options.misconception: reads the examination as a test of reading speed rather than of recall and use

The first option says both. The second substitutes a different aim and a different remedy, and feedback on written work improves writing. The third makes the allocation the challenge, and a scheme that does not resolve it can be revised. The fourth turns the examination into a reading test, which a prepared student does not need to be.
questions.hint: Ask what the student has to do in the first ten minutes of the examination.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What an essay plan makes visible
questions.learningObjective: say what a plan reveals about an argument, then what it cannot show
questions.stem: A student submits an essay plan before drafting. First say what a plan makes visible that a finished draft conceals, then say what it cannot show.

options.text: Which premises carry the argument and in what order, and whether the argument holds once those premises are written out
How fluent the sentences will be, and how many words the finished essay will run to
options.misconception: offers things a plan cannot reveal and a draft would reveal well enough

options.text: How the evidence will be set out, and whether the argument would survive the evidence as it stands
options.misconception: divides the two things wrongly, since whether the argument survives the evidence is exactly what the premises and their order settle

options.text: Whether the topic has been understood, and whether the reading supports the approach taken
options.misconception: treats a plan as a test of understanding rather than of the argument it is meant to organise

questions.explanation: A finished draft reads smoothly whether or not it holds, and its most consequential features, the premises it silently relies on and the order it puts them in, are the things a reader cannot extract without effort. questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Why a criterion has to point at something in the text
questions.learningObjective: justify a rubric criterion's dependence on an observable in the submitted work
questions.stem: Explain why a rubric criterion has to name something in the submitted text that a marker can point to, rather than a quality the marker is asked to judge.

answer.exemplar: A criterion exists to make marking repeatable, and repeatability is bought by tying the mark to something in the work rather than to a marker's reading of it, because two markers asked whether a piece of work is thoughtful will produce two answers and neither will be able to say what the other missed. Naming an observable does not make the judgement mechanical, and it should not, since the marker still has to decide what counts as an instance of the quality. It makes the disagreement locatable. When a marker says the third paragraph does not connect the evidence to the claim, the student can look at the third paragraph and see the claim, the evidence, and the missing step between them, and can decide whether the objection is fair. Where the criterion says only that the work should be analytical, the same student can only ask what the marker wanted, and the usual answer is more analysis, which is not a description of anything. The observable also protects the marker, because a student who disputes the mark has to argue with a reading of the work rather than with a preference, and a marker who cannot produce a place in the text has conceded that the mark was a judgement of the student rather than of the essay. This is why a criterion is often written as a quality plus a place: the quality says what is being looked for and the place says where to look, and a criterion with only the first is a description of an aspiration while a criterion with only the second is a checklist. The test is a practical one. Give two markers the same criterion and the same essay and ask each to name where the criterion was met. Where they can point to the same two paragraphs, the criterion is doing its work. Where one points to the introduction and the other to the conclusion, the criterion has told them to have a preference rather than to read.

questions.explanation: A strong response explains that naming an observable makes the marker's judgement checkable against the text, locates any disagreement between markers, and stops a criterion operating as a preference.
questions.hint: Ask two markers to point to where a quality-only criterion was met in one essay.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What makes a comment worth writing
questions.learningObjective: justify judging a comment by what it makes possible for the student to do next
questions.stem: Explain why the usefulness of a comment is best judged by what it makes possible for the student to do next, rather than by how much it describes the work.

answer.exemplar: A comment is read by someone who has to do something after reading it, and the only thing that matters is what that something can be. This is why a comment that describes a fault accurately can be close to useless: a student who is told that a paragraph lacks a connection between evidence and claim now knows the location and the diagnosis, and the hard part, which is deciding what the connection should be and whether one can be made at all in the space available, is handed back to the person least equipped for it. The same student, told that the paragraph should state the rule that would carry the reader from the number to the claim, has an operation to carry out and can attempt it, discover whether the claim will bear it, and bring back a specific question. That is the difference the next step makes visible, because an attempt produces a question and a diagnosis does not. Judging a comment by how much it describes therefore rewards a skill markers are good at, which is reading, over the skill students need, which is deciding what to do. It also produces comments that grow longer as the work is marked more thoroughly, which is a sign that length and usefulness have come apart. The test is worth stating plainly: a student who follows a comment and does not know what to do next has been failed by it, whatever the comment said about the essay. This is not an argument for narrow comments, since a comment that leaves out a problem the student cannot see is also a failure, and a student cannot act on a fault they have not identified. The requirement is that the comment and the student's capacity have to meet: enough description to locate and understand the fault, and enough operation to act on it. Where a comment cannot supply the second without the first, it should be split, with the diagnostic part returned for a conversation and the operational part written down. The reason this matters beyond tidiness is that a student who has revised once on a useful comment knows what revision feels like and will try again, while a student who has revised once on a comment that described a problem without a route has learned that revision is not something they can do.

questions.explanation: A strong response explains that a diagnosis without an operation returns the hard part of revision to the student, that attempting an operation produces a further question, and that a comment should be judged by whether the student can act after reading it.
questions.hint: Ask what a student would do next after reading a comment that named a fault and nothing else.

questions.learningObjective: state a claim as a testable proposition, then name the strongest objection to it
questions.stem: A student's claim is that a new reporting requirement has made the district's meetings shorter. First state the claim as a testable proposition, then say the strongest objection to it.

options.text: That the meetings are shorter in clock time, and that a requirement which adds paperwork would more plausibly lengthen the preparation and reorder the agenda
That the meetings are shorter in clock time, and that nobody has yet measured the length of any meeting in the district
options.misconception: presses the absence of a measurement instead of the reasoning, and the claim could be tested tomorrow

options.text: That the meetings are shorter in the sense of fewer items discussed, and that reporting requirements rarely change an agenda
options.misconception: restates the claim in a second sense and objects to a general tendency rather than to this case

options.text: That the requirement shortened the meetings, and that the district's custom of ending on time accounts for the effect
options.misconception: offers a rival explanation in place of an objection, and the claim is left with nothing opposing it

questions.explanation: A claim becomes testable when it is stated in terms something could come out against, and the strongest objection is the one that attacks the reasoning rather than the evidence's absence or the wording, which here is that a requirement generating paperwork is a reason to expect more preparation time and a reworked agenda, not less. The first option says both. The second objects that no one has measured anything, which is a reason to measure rather than a reason against the claim. The third shifts the sense of shorter and then objects to a general tendency. The fourth supplies a competing cause and calls it an objection, which leaves the original claim unopposed.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would expect to happen if the claim were not true of the meetings.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A self-rating and the check that makes it mean something
questions.learningObjective: say what makes a self-rating meaningful, then what would bring it into line with a marker's
questions.stem: Before submitting, a student rates a draft as meeting the top level of every criterion. First say what would have to be examined for that rating to mean anything, then say what would bring it into line with a marker's rating.

options.text: Whether a place in the draft can be pointed to for each criterion, and the description of the level the draft actually meets
The grade awarded in the previous term, and a comparison between that grade and the rating given to this draft
options.misconception: anchors the rating in the reader's history rather than in the level descriptions the rubric uses

options.text: The reading list, and whether every source on it is cited somewhere in the draft
options.misconception: supplies an input check in place of a comparison with a level description

options.text: The word count, and whether the draft reaches the length the top level is described at
options.misconception: measures a level by length, which no level description in the rubric does

questions.explanation: A rating becomes a judgement rather than a mood when a place in the draft can be named for each criterion, and the calibration comes from comparing that with the description of the level the work actually shows, which is the comparison the exercise exists to produce. The first option says that. The second sets the draft against a past grade, which is a different reference and one the student controls in the way they read their own history. The third checks the inputs rather than the work. The fourth measures a level by its length, and a length is not what a level describes.
questions.hint: Ask what a student would have to name in the draft to defend the rating.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A claim and an effect that stopped
questions.learningObjective: report an effect whose duration is part of what was found
questions.stem: A report claims a notice reduced late arrivals. Records show arrivals fell by a sixth in the notice's first month and then held at the new level for five months. Which treatment of the evidence is sound?

options.text: Report the fall together with its duration, and treat the notice as a candidate explanation for the first month rather than for the period as a whole
Report the total fall across the six months, since the level held afterwards is part of the same effect
options.misconception: adds the sustained level to the initial fall as though a continuing level were continuing change

options.text: Leave the notice out of the account, since an effect that stops is not an effect at all
options.misconception: requires a permanent change before a temporary one will count, which is a stricter test than the claim makes

options.text: Report the fall and attribute it to the notice, since nothing else happened in the same month to account for it
options.misconception: accepts the coincidence of timing as the whole of a causal account

questions.explanation: The records show a fall and then a level, and those are two findings rather than one, and the report's job is to say that the notice is a candidate explanation for the change in the first month while the persistence of the new level is something else, whose cause the report would have to look for separately. The first option says that. The second counts the sustained level as part of the effect, and a level that holds is not a fall continuing. The third discards the notice for the effect's stopping, which overstates the requirement: a claim about a change in a level does not need that level to move again. The fourth attributes the whole six months to the notice on the strength of the first month, which is the claim the evidence cannot carry.
questions.hint: Ask whether the records show a change or a level, and for how long each lasts.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Two works either side of a mark boundary
questions.learningObjective: infer what a marker was measuring from a boundary applied to similar work
questions.stem: Two essays sit either side of a mark boundary, one just above and one just below, and both make the same central move. What does that show about the mark?

options.text: That the mark is responding to something other than the move both essays make, such as their polish or their length
That the marker is inconsistent, since two works that make the same move should receive the same mark
options.misconception: calls the outcome inconsistent without asking what the marker is measuring

options.text: That the boundary should be removed, since a single mark cannot separate works this similar
options.misconception: proposes deleting the boundary rather than finding out what it is marking

options.text: That the two essays are not in fact similar, since a marker reads closely enough to tell
options.misconception: presumes a reading error to protect the marker's account of the work

questions.explanation: When two works that do the same central thing receive different marks, the difference has to be located somewhere, and the candidates are the features the marker is in fact responding to, which may be polish, length or an unstated sense of the level, rather than the argument. The first option says that. The second uses the word inconsistent to avoid the question of what was measured, and inconsistency is a conclusion rather than a description. The third proposes removing the boundary, which would leave the same undisclosed measure operating everywhere. The fourth assumes the marker is right and the similarity is illusory, which is a way of closing the question without opening it.
questions.hint: Ask what could differ between the two essays other than the move they make.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a marking workload does to the marks
questions.learningObjective: predict how a marking constraint affects the distribution of marks
questions.stem: A marker has three hours for forty submissions, works through the first ten with care and marks the remaining thirty at a glance. What is the most likely effect on the marks?

options.text: The mark comes to reflect where a submission sat in the pile, because the closeness of reading that separates the work changes partway through
The first ten are treated unfairly, since they received more of the marker's attention than the rest
options.misconception: puts the disadvantage at the wrong end of the ordering

options.text: The scheme should be replaced, since a scheme that cannot be applied with care should not be used
options.misconception: proposes abandoning the scheme rather than changing the conditions under which it is applied

options.text: The first ten are the strongest submissions, since a marker reads carefully what deserves careful reading
options.misconception: attributes a quality to a position in the pile and so explains the pattern by the work rather than by the reading

questions.explanation: A mark is partly a function of how closely a work was read, so a queue in which the first submissions get careful reading and the rest do not distributes marks by queue position as well as by quality, and the effect appears as a fall in the marks that is not explained by the work. The first option says that. The second has the direction backwards. The third proposes a new scheme, when the problem is the ratio of time to submissions rather than the scheme's design. The fourth explains the pattern by the merit of the early work, which would have produced the same pattern under any queueing and so explains nothing.
questions.hint: Ask how closely each submission was read, and what a close read can detect that a glance cannot.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A comment that rewards a claim nothing can count against
questions.learningObjective: identify a marking comment that cannot be acted on or disputed
questions.stem: A comment tells a student to engage more deeply with the material rather than summarising it. What is the problem with the comment as guidance?

options.text: It can neither be acted on nor disputed, since no work is deeper than every other work and no result settles whether it is deep enough
It is unfair, since depth is not a reasonable demand on a student working to a word limit
options.misconception: attacks the demand as unreasonable rather than as unmeasurable

options.text: It should use the rubric's own wording, so the comment ought to be rewritten in the level descriptions
options.misconception: prescribes a change of vocabulary and leaves the demand unmeasurable in either vocabulary

options.text: It is too demanding, since work of any depth is beyond most submissions
options.misconception: judges the demand by how few students meet it, which is a question about the cohort rather than about the comment

questions.explanation: Guidance is usable when a student can either carry it out or show that it has been carried out, and a demand for greater depth satisfies neither test, since the work cannot be shown to meet it and no reading of it can show that it falls short, which is the same problem as a claim that cannot be refuted. The first option says that. The second calls the demand unreasonable, which is a different objection and one a rubric can answer by lowering it. The third asks for different words, and the words do not change whether a degree can be shown. The fourth measures the demand against the cohort, which says how hard it feels rather than whether it means anything.
questions.hint: Ask what a student would point at to show the demand had been met.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a portfolio of final versions cannot show
questions.learningObjective: identify the evidence a portfolio excludes when only finished work is submitted
questions.stem: A portfolio contains a polished final version of a project, with every earlier draft removed. What can that portfolio not show?

options.text: How the work developed, since a sequence of drafts is what would show the decisions taken and the corrections made
The quality of the final version, since a polished text is evidence of its own quality
options.misconception: denies a portfolio the one thing it does provide

options.text: That the work was the student's, since authorship is established by the polish of the final version
options.misconception: treats polish as proof of authorship, and polish is available to a writer of any ability

options.text: Whether the work met the criteria, since criteria are written for drafts rather than for finished pieces
options.misconception: denies that criteria apply to submitted work, which is the only kind of work that is assessed

questions.explanation: What a project was made of includes the choices it went through, and those are recorded in the sequence of versions rather than in the last one, so a portfolio of finals keeps the outcome and discards the process that a criterion about development would be applied to. The first option says that. The second denies the portfolio its evident strength, since a polished text does speak well of the work that is in front of the reader. The third infers authorship from polish, and polish is a feature of presentation available at every level of ability. The fourth says criteria are for drafts, and the criteria in a portfolio are applied to whatever the student submits.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader learns from a fourth version that they do not learn from the last one.
